nodes.name: Open-loop Reference Model (ORM)-adaptive system
nodes.statement: We denote the underlying open--loop systems in all these cases as {\em Open-loop Reference Model} (ORM)--adaptive systems.

nodes.name: Combined/composite Model Reference Adaptive Control (CMRAC)
nodes.statement: Another class of adaptive systems that have been explored in the past where a noticeable improvement in transient performance was obtained is in the context of {\em Combined/composite direct and indirect Model Reference Adaptive Control} (CMRAC) \cite{duarte1989combined,slotine1989composite}.
nodes.statement_short: CMRAC: combined direct and indirect model reference adaptive control, known for improved transients.

nodes.name: CMRAC with Closed-loop reference models (CMRAC-C)
nodes.statement: The resulting {\em CMRAC with Closed-loop reference models} (CMRAC-C) are shown to be stable, enable the feedback of noise-free state estimates while guaranteeing stability, and most importantly are shown to have guaranteed transient properties.

nodes.name: Linear plant with scalar input
nodes.statement: Consider the linear system dynamics with scalar input \begin{equation} \dot x(t) = A_p x(t) + b u(t) \end{equation} where ${x(t) \in \mathbb R^n}$ is the state vector, ${u(t)\in \mathbb R}$ is the control input, ${A_p\in \mathbb R^{n \times n}}$ is unknown and ${b\in \mathbb R^n}$ is known.
nodes.statement_short: Plant $\dot x = A_p x + b u$ with unknown $A_p$ and known $b$.

nodes.name: Plant dynamics
nodes.statement: \dot x(t) = A_p x(t) + b u(t)
nodes.label: s1:sys

nodes.name: Closed-loop reference model dynamics
nodes.statement: Our goal is to design the control input such that ${x(t)}$ follows the reference model state ${x_m(t)\in \mathbb R^n}$ defined by the following dynamics \begin{equation} \dot x_m(t) = A_m x_m(t) + b r(t) - L(x(t)-x_m(t)) \end{equation} where ${A_m \in \mathbb R^{n\times n }}$ is Hurwtitz and ${r(t)\in \mathbb R}$ is a bounded possible time varying reference command.
nodes.statement_short: Reference model $\dot x_m = A_m x_m + b r - L(x - x_m)$ with Hurwitz $A_m$ and bounded command $r$.

nodes.name: Closed-loop reference model (CRM)
nodes.statement: \dot x_m(t) = A_m x_m(t) + b r(t) - L(x(t)-x_m(t))
nodes.label: s1:ref

nodes.name: Luenberger gain
nodes.statement: ${L\in \mathbb R^{n\times n}}$ is denoted as the {\em Luenberger--gain}, and is chosen such that \begin{equation} \bar A_m \triangleq A_m+L \end{equation} is Hurwitz.

nodes.name: Closed-loop reference matrix $\bar A_m$
nodes.statement: \bar A_m \triangleq A_m+L
nodes.label: s1:ambar

nodes.name: Closed-loop Reference Model (CRM)
nodes.statement: Equation \eqref{s1:ref} is referred to as a CRM, and when ${L=0}$ the classical ORM is recovered.

nodes.name: Matching condition
nodes.statement: A parameter vector ${\theta^*\in\mathbb R^n}$ exists that satisfies the {\em matching condition} \begin{equation} A_m=A_p+b\theta^{*T}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: asm:m

nodes.name: Matching condition $A_m=A_p+b\theta^{*T}$
nodes.statement: A_m=A_p+b\theta^{*T}.
nodes.label: s1:match

nodes.name: Adaptive control law and Lyapunov matrix
nodes.statement: The control input is chosen in the form \begin{equation} u(t)= \theta^T(t) x(t) + r(t) \end{equation} where $\theta(t) \in \mathbb R^n$ is the adaptive control gain with the update law \begin{equation} \dot \theta(t) = -\Gamma x(t)e^T(t) Pb \end{equation} with ${\Gamma = \Gamma^T>0}$, ${e(t)= x(t)-x_m(t)}$ is the model following error and $P=P^T>0$ is the solution to the algebraic Lyapunov equation \begin{equation} \bar A_m^TP+P \bar A_m = -I_{n\times n}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Control $u=\theta^T x + r$, gradient update law for $\theta$, model following error $e=x-x_m$, and $P$ solving the Lyapunov equation for $\bar A_m$.

nodes.name: Control input
nodes.statement: u(t)= \theta^T(t) x(t) + r(t)
nodes.label: s1:u

nodes.name: Adaptive update law
nodes.statement: \dot \theta(t) = -\Gamma x(t)e^T(t) Pb
nodes.label: s1:law

nodes.name: Algebraic Lyapunov equation
nodes.statement: \bar A_m^TP+P \bar A_m = -I_{n\times n}.
nodes.label: s1:lyap

nodes.name: Error model and parameter error
nodes.statement: The underlying error model in this case is given by \begin{equation}\dot e(t)= \bar A_m e(t) + b \tilde\theta(t)x(t) \end{equation} where ${\tilde\theta(t)=\theta(t)-\theta^*}$ is the parameter error.

nodes.name: Error model dynamics
nodes.statement: \dot e(t)= \bar A_m e(t) + b \tilde\theta(t)x(t)
nodes.label: s1:et

nodes.name: Global stability of the CRM-adaptive system
nodes.statement: The closed-loop adaptive system with \eqref{s1:sys}, \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s1:u} and \eqref{s1:law} is globally stable with $e(t)$ tending to zero asymptotically, under the matching condition in \eqref{s1:match}.
conclusions: is globally stable with $e(t)$ tending to zero asymptotically
nodes.label: thm:simple

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: It is straight forward to show using \eqref{s1:law} and \eqref{s1:et} that \begin{equation} V(e,\tilde\theta) = e^TPe + \tilde \theta^T \Gamma^{-1} \tilde \theta \end{equation} is a Lyapunov function. Since $e$ is bounded, the structure of \eqref{s1:ref} implies that $x_m$ is bounded. $x$ in turn and $u$ are bounded. Barbalat lemma ensures asymptotic convergence of $e(t)$ to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Lyapunov function $V=e^TPe+\tilde\theta^T\Gamma^{-1}\tilde\theta$, boundedness of signals, then Barbalat's lemma.

nodes.name: Lyapunov function $V(e,\tilde\theta)$
nodes.statement: V(e,\tilde\theta) = e^TPe + \tilde \theta^T \Gamma^{-1} \tilde \theta
nodes.label: can

nodes.name: Finite convergence time $T(\epsilon,L)$
nodes.statement: For all $\epsilon>0$ there exists $T(\epsilon,L)>0$ such that $t\geq T(\epsilon,L)$ implies $\norms{e(t)}\leq \epsilon$.
conclusions: For all $\epsilon>0$ there exists $T(\epsilon,L)>0$ such that $t\geq T(\epsilon,L)$ implies $\norms{e(t)}\leq \epsilon$.
nodes.label: Tdef

nodes.name: CRM-adaptive system
nodes.statement: The overall CRM--adaptive system is defined by \eqref{s1:sys}, \eqref{s1:ref}, \eqref{s1:u}, and \eqref{s1:law}.

nodes.name: Open-loop reference model and true tracking error $e^o$
nodes.statement: The standard open-loop reference model is given by \begin{equation}\dot x_m^o(t) = A_m x_m^o(t) + b r(t) \end{equation} with the corresponding tracking error \begin{equation} e^o(t) = x(t) - x_m^o(t) . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Open-loop reference model
nodes.statement: \dot x_m^o(t) = A_m x_m^o(t) + b r(t)
nodes.label: eo

nodes.name: True tracking error $e^o$
nodes.statement: e^o(t) = x(t) - x_m^o(t) .
nodes.label: eodef

nodes.name: True tracking error and pseudo-tracking error
nodes.statement: One can in fact view the error $e^o$ as the {\em true tracking error} and $e$ as a pseudo--tracking error.

nodes.name: Convergence of $x$ to the open-loop reference state
nodes.statement: The state vector $x(t)$ converges to $x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.
conclusions: The state vector $x(t)$ converges to $x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{thm:simple} we can conclude that $e(t)\rightarrow0$ asymptotically. Thus we can conclude that $x_m(t) \rightarrow x_m^o(t)$ as $e(t)\rightarrow 0$, implying that $e^o\rightarrow 0$, thus $x(t)\rightarrow x_m^o(t)$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: From Theorem 1, $e\to0$, hence $x_m\to x_m^o$ and $x\to x_m^o$.

nodes.name: CRM makes the reference model nonlinear
nodes.statement: The choice of the CRM as in (2) essentially makes the reference model nonlinear, as $x$ depends on $\theta$ which in turn depends on $x_m$ in a highly nonlinear manner. In general, the tracking problem in a ORM--adaptive system can be viewed as one where an overall nonlinear time-varying system is to be designed such that its output tracks that of a linear time-invariant system. The CRM-adaptive system is one where the overall nonlinear system is instead required to follow a nonlinear (reference) model. This nonlinear model, however, is chosen such that it asymptotically approaches the original linear reference model in the classical case, and hence the CRM-adaptive system retains all the desired characteristics of the ORM-adaptive system. As we will show in Section \ref{section:perf}, the CRM-adaptive system has an additional desirable property, of quantifiable transient properties, which the ORM-adaptive system may not necessarily possess. We will also show in this section that this is made possible by virtue of the additional degree of freedom available to the adaptive system in the form of the feedback gain in the CRM.
nodes.statement_short: The CRM is a nonlinear reference model that asymptotically approaches the linear ORM, retaining its properties and adding quantifiable transients.

nodes.name: Spectral constants $\sigma$, $s$, $a$ and gains $L$, $\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Given a Hurwtiz matrix $A_m\in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ \begin{equation} \begin{split} \sigma& \triangleq - \max_i \left( \text{real} (\lambda_i(A_m)) \right) \\ s& \triangleq - \min_i \left( \lambda_i\left(A_m+A_m^T\right)/2 \right) \\ a& \triangleq \norms{A_m}. \end{split} \end{equation} For ease of exposition, throughout the paper, we choose $L$ in \eqref{s1:ref} and $\Gamma$ in \eqref{s2:adaplaw} as follows: \begin{align} L &\triangleq -\ell I_{n \times n} \\ \Gamma & \triangleq \gamma I_{n\times n}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma$ = minus the largest real part of eigenvalues of $A_m$, $s$ = minus the smallest eigenvalue of its symmetric part, $a=\|A_m\|$; $L=-\ell I$, $\Gamma=\gamma I$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: $A_m$ is Hurwitz and therefore $\sigma>0$. It is not necessary however that the sum $A_m+A_m^T$ is Hurwitz. The trace operator is denoted as $\text{Tr} (\cdot)$ and is a linear operator. Recalling that a matrix and its transpose have the same trace we can conclude that $\Sigma _i \lambda_i(A_m) =\Sigma _i \lambda_i(A_m+A_m^T)/2$. Finally we have that \begin{equation*} s \geq -\frac 1 {2n} \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\left(A_m+A_m^T\right) = -\frac 1 n \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i(A_m) \geq \sigma>0. \ \relax \end{equation*} \let\IEEEQED\relax
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma>0$ since $A_m$ is Hurwitz; trace equality gives $s\ge$ average eigenvalue $\ge\sigma$.

nodes.name: Free design parameters $\ell$ and $\ell/\gamma$
nodes.statement: In this section it is argued that the free design parameters for the adaptive system are $\ell$ and the ratio of $\ell$ and $\gamma$. It is clear from \eqref{V_1} that the rate of exponential decay of the Lyapunov function is solely a function of the slowest eigenvalue of $\sigma$ and $\ell$. The term $\sigma$ is defined by the open--loop reference model jacobiam $A_m$ in \eqref{s1:ref} and cannot be independently increased without also increasing the bound on $\theta^*$, due to the fact that $A_m= A_p+b\theta^{*T}$ from \eqref{s1:match}. Therfore, from \eqref{alpha1} it is clear that while increasing $\sigma$ increases $\alpha_1$ it also increases the size of of the compact set $\mathcal E$ that the model following error is exponentially converging to. The Luenberger gain $\ell$, in contrast, does not affect the matching condition for the adaptive system and therefore increasing $\ell$ does not result in a high--gain matching condition. It is seen from \eqref{b1} that while increasing $\ell$ may result in a larger $\alpha_1$ which is desirable, it also increases the $\alpha_2$ and $\beta_1$. At first glance this seems undesirable. However, it is important to note that $\ell$ is inversely proportional to the bounds for $P$ in \eqref{s1:pbound} and \eqref{minP}. Upon further inspection of the tuning law in \eqref{s2:adaplaw}, when Projeciton is not active the adaptive law reduces to \begin{equation*} \dot\theta= -\gamma x e^T P b, \end{equation*} and therefore, the only fixed parameters that control the rate of adaptation are $\gamma, P(\ell)$ and $b$. Given that $b$ is fixed it is ignored and thus the learning rate is a function of $\gamma \norms P $. Therefore, if $\gamma$ and $\ell$ are increased at the same rate, the effective rate of change in the adaptive tuning law will remain the same, which illustrates that the ratio of $\ell$ and $\gamma$ is an important design parameter.

nodes.statement: The bounds on $e(t)$ and the $\mathcal L_2$--norm of $\dot\theta$ directly show that CRM--adaptive systems lead to smaller $e(t)$ than with the ORM which are obtained by setting $\ell=0$ in \eqref{e2e} and \eqref{el2}. This indicates that there is a trade-off between fast transients and true tracking error. The signal that succinctly captures this trade off is $\dot u$, whose behavior is captured in detail using the time intervals $\mathbb T1$, $\mathbb T2$, and $\mathbb T3$. We also showed in Theorem \ref{thmpopt} that this trade-off can be optimized via a suitable choice of $\ell$ and $\rho$. nodes.name: Comparison of CRM and ORM bounds on $\dot u$
nodes.statement: We now compare the bounds on $\dot u$ using observations (A1)--(A3) and (B1)--(B3). In order to have the same basis for comparison, we assume that $\gamma$, $\sigma$, and $\ell$ are such that $\rho=\rho_0$ and that both CRM-- and ORM--adaptive systems start with the same bound at $t=0$. As noted above, a tight bound cannot be derived for the ORM-based adaptive system over $[N\tau_1^*,N\tau_2^\prime)$. In the best scenario, one can assume that this bound is no larger than that over $[0,N\tau_1^*]$. This allows us to derive the bounds shown in Figure \ref{fig:udot}. The main observations that one can make from this figure are summarized below: \begin{itemize} \item Even though at time $t = 0$, both the ORM and CRM have the same bound, since $\tau_1$ can be made much smaller than $\tau_2^\prime$, this bound is valid for a much shorter time with the CRM-system than in the ORM--system. This helps us conclude that the initial transients can be made to subside much faster in the former case than the latter, by suitably choosing $\ell$. \item The bound on $\dot u$ for $\mathbb T_2$ with the CRM--adaptive system is however linear in powers of $\ell$ and hence can be larger than the bound on $\dot u$ with the ORM-adaptive system over $\mathbb T_2^\prime$. \item The above observations clearly illustrate, if the cost function $U(N\tau_2^\prime;\rho,\ell)$ is minimized then the CRM system will have smoother transients than the ORM. Then, at larger times the error dynamics will asymptotically converges to zero. \end{itemize}

In Region 1, the adaptive system is subjected to non--zero initial conditions in the state and the reference input is zero. At $t=10$ sec, the beginning of Region 2, a filtered step input is introduced. At $t=20$ sec In Region 3, time-variations in the plant parameter as well, disturbances and a filtered step input are introduced. Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the response of the CRM--adaptive system over 0 to 35 seconds, with $x_m$, $x$, and $e$ indicated in Figure 2, and $u$, $\dot u$, and $\theta$ indicated in Figure 3. In both cases, the resulting performance is compared with the classical adaptive system. The first point that should be noted is a satisfactory behavior in the steady-state of the CRM--adaptive controller. In particular, as can be seen from the latter half of Region 1, both $e$ and $e^o$ tend to zero as $t$ approaches 10 seconds. The same satisfactory trends are observed in regions 2 and 3 as well, underscoring the robustness property of CRM--adaptive control, which validates Theorem 2. We also note yet another significant difference between the responses of CRM--adaptive control and the classical one, which pertains to the rate of control input $\dot u$. An examination of Regions 2 and 3 clearly illustrates that the control input is smoother for CRM--adaptive control.

nodes.name: Speculation on why CMRAC improves transients
nodes.statement: While the above analysis does not directly support the observed transient improvements with CMRAC, we provide a few speculations below: The free design parameter $L_i$ in the identifier is typically chosen to have eigenvalues faster than the plant that is being controlled. Therefore the identification model following error $e_i$ converges rapidly and $\hat\theta(t)$ will have smooth transients. It can be argued that the desirable transient properties of the identifier pass on to the direct component through the tuning law, and in particular $\epsilon_\theta$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5(ii)
nodes.statement: Let $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$ be a normalized eigenvector of $P$. By pre-- and postmultiplying \eqref{s1:lyap} by $\xi^T$ and $\xi$, we have \begin{equation*} \xi^T \bar A_m^TP \xi + \xi^T P\bar A_m \xi =- \xi^TI_{n\times n} \xi \end{equation*} which reduces to \begin{equation*} \lambda_i (P) \xi^T (\bar A_m +\bar A_m^T)\xi =-1. \end{equation*} Expanding $\bar A_m$ we have \begin{equation*} \lambda_i (P) \xi^T ( A_m + A_m^T-2 l I_{n\times n }) \xi =-1. \end{equation*} Finally, using the definitions in \eqref{s1:ambound} and taking the minimum eigenvalue of $P$ we arrive at \eqref{minP} \cite{mor84}.

Consider the function \begin{equation} F(\theta)= f(\theta)^2,\end{equation} and taking its time derivative \begin{equation*} \dot F(\theta) = 2f(\theta)(\nabla f(\theta))^T\dot \theta \end{equation*} and when $f(\theta)=1$ one has that \begin{equation*} \dot F(\theta) = 2f(\theta) \left(\nabla f(\theta)\right)^T\text{Proj}_\Gamma(\theta,y,f). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Invariance
nodes.statement: With direct substitution of the operator in \eqref{eq:proj_vec_gamma} one finds that \begin{equation} {(\nabla f(\theta))^T\text{Proj}_\Gamma(\theta,y,f)\leq0}\end{equation} whenever $f(\theta)=1$, and thus \eqref{apptheta} holds.

Lets consider the case where $\theta(t)$ is on the boundary of $\mathcal D_1$ and thus $f(\theta)=1$ and $\hat \theta \subseteq \mathcal D_1$.

nodes.name: Factorisation
nodes.statement: Due to our choice of $L$, $A_m$ and $L$ commute, thus ${\exp(A_m+L)=\exp(A_m)\exp(L)}$ and \begin{equation*} P = \int_0^\infty \exp(A_m^T\tau) \exp(L^T\tau) \exp(A_m \tau)\exp(L \tau)\ d\tau. \end{equation*}
